result: The manuscript establishes the clinical context and motivation for studying EEG patterns in infants under anesthesia. It states that 200,000 children receive general anesthesia in the first year of life in the US, that anesthetics act in the brain and spinal cord to produce anesthetic states, and that EEG-derived indices developed in adults are inaccurate in infants and younger children.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Rabbitts et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2010, 2011; Ching and Brown, 2014; Davidson, 2007; Constant and Sabourdin, 2012). These claims provide well-established background knowledge that motivates the study.

result: During maintenance of sevoflurane anesthesia (MOSSA), slow-delta oscillations were present at all ages (0-6 months), while theta and alpha oscillations emerged around 4 months of age. Frontal EEG power was significantly greater across all frequencies in 4-6 month-old infants compared to 0-3 month-old infants. Unlike adults, all infants lacked frontal alpha predominance and coherence.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C12-C18, and C56-C58 are consistently supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3-6 and statistical analyses with 95% CI bootstrap methods (Figure 4B-E). The findings show clear age-dependent differences in EEG spectral features during MOSSA, with appropriate statistical support for group comparisons.

result: End-tidal sevoflurane requirements during MOSSA were significantly lower in infants 0-3 months compared to infants 4-6 months of age.
evaluation: Claim C19 is supported by clinical data in Table 1 showing median end-tidal sevoflurane of 2.0% (95% CI: 0.8-2.6%) for 0-3 months vs 2.6% (95% CI: 2.4-3.1%) for 4-6 months, with p=0.002. The authors appropriately conducted a secondary analysis at identical sevoflurane concentrations (1.8%) to control for potential dose effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

result: Spatial analysis of EEG power during MOSSA revealed that slow and delta oscillations were broadly distributed across the scalp in all infants, with lower power along the midline. Alpha oscillations in 4-6 month-old infants were distributed more laterally. Unlike adults, infants 0-3 months showed no frontal predominance of alpha power, and a small but significant frontal alpha predominance began to emerge at 4-6 months of age.
evaluation: Claims C20-C26 and C59-C61 are supported by topographic mapping data (Figures 5-7) and statistical analyses using 95% CI paired bootstrap methods. The findings demonstrate age-dependent spatial differences in EEG patterns, though the frontal alpha predominance in 4-6 month infants is described as 'small but significant,' indicating an emerging rather than fully developed feature.

result: Frontal coherence analysis showed high coherence (~0.6) in slow and delta frequency ranges for all infants during MOSSA, with peak coherence at 1.0 Hz in both age groups. However, despite strong theta and alpha power in 4-6 month-old infants, these oscillations were not coherent, contrasting with adults who show strong frontal alpha coherence during sevoflurane anesthesia.
evaluation: Claims C27-C33 are supported by coherence analysis data (Figure 8) and statistical comparisons using 95% CI bootstrap analysis. The findings demonstrate coordinated local frontal slow/delta oscillations across all ages, but absence of frontal alpha coherence even in older infants, which differs from adult patterns (Akeju et al., 2014c).

result: Global coherence analysis revealed weak coherence (<0.2) across all frequency bands for all infants during MOSSA, despite the presence of slow, delta, theta, and alpha oscillations in the spectrograms. This contrasts with adults who show highly coordinated, coherent frontal alpha activity during propofol anesthesia, though the lack of slow/delta coherence is consistent with adult patterns.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by global coherence data (Figure 9C) and appropriate citations to adult studies (Cimenser et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2012; Purdon et al., 2013; Akeju et al., 2014c). The findings demonstrate fundamental differences in spatial coordination of EEG oscillations between infants and adults.

result: During the awake state, slow and delta power with low theta and alpha power were predominant at all ages, with significantly lower power across all frequencies in 0-3 month-old infants compared to 4-6 month-old infants. When comparing awake state to MOSSA, slow and delta power remained relatively constant in all infants. Infants 0-3 months showed no change in theta or alpha activity with anesthesia, while infants 4-6 months showed significant increases in theta and alpha power during MOSSA compared to awake state.
evaluation: Claims C37-C43 and C62 are supported by experimental data (Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1) and statistical analyses using 95% CI bootstrap and paired bootstrap methods. The findings demonstrate age-dependent EEG responses to anesthesia, with state-specific spectral changes emerging at 4-6 months of age.

result: During emergence from sevoflurane anesthesia, infants began displaying gross body movement at median end-tidal concentrations of 0.6% (0-3 months) and 0.4% (4-6 months), with no movement at ≥1.2% sevoflurane. Slow and delta power remained constant during emergence in all ages. Infants 0-3 months showed no clear associations between EEG power and sevoflurane concentration or movement recovery. In contrast, infants 4-6 months showed that theta and alpha power decreased with decreasing sevoflurane concentration below 1.2%, reaching negligible levels when >50% of infants displayed movement. Unlike adults, there was no spatial shift in alpha activity during emergence.
evaluation: Claims C44-C55 and C63 are supported by experimental data (Figures 11-12) and statistical analyses using 95% CI paired bootstrap methods. The findings demonstrate age-dependent EEG dynamics during emergence, with dose-dependent changes in theta/alpha power only in older infants. The contrast with adult patterns (anteriorization reversal) is appropriately cited (Ní Mhuircheartaigh et al., 2013; Purdon et al., 2013).

result: In infants 4-6 months of age, alpha power was greatest during maintenance compared to awake and emergence states, and theta and alpha power decreased with decreasing sevoflurane concentration during emergence.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by experimental data in Figures 10-12 showing state-dependent changes in alpha power. These claims summarize key findings about alpha power dynamics across anesthetic states in older infants.

result: The observed EEG dynamic differences between infant age groups are attributed to developmental factors including regional differences in synaptogenesis, glucose metabolism, and myelination across the cortex. The neuroanatomy and neurophysiology suggest that thalamocortical connections required for alpha oscillations are absent in 0-3 month-old infants but present in 4-6 month-old infants, and that differential thalamic connectivity for frontal alpha predominance is not present in infants ≤6 months. The appearance of alpha oscillations at 4 months may indicate an important developmental milestone in processes guided by subplate neurons.
evaluation: Claims C9, C84-C92, and C94 are largely inferential and speculative, drawing on developmental neuroscience literature (Brody et al., 1987; Kinney et al., 1988; Huttenlocher et al., 1982; Johnson, 2001; Chugani and Phelps, 1986; Chugani et al., 1987; Kinnala et al., 1996; Kanold and Luhmann, 2010) to explain the observed EEG patterns. While the developmental explanations are plausible and well-cited, they remain hypotheses that are not directly tested in this study. The mechanistic links between developmental changes and EEG patterns are inferred rather than demonstrated.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on adult EEG patterns under anesthesia, including that adults show incoherent slow oscillations and coherent frontal alpha oscillations under propofol and ether-derived anesthetics, that alpha oscillations are thalamocortical in origin, and that anteriorization occurs with frontal alpha disappearing and posterior alpha reappearing during recovery of consciousness. Modeling studies suggest mechanisms involving differential effects on thalamic nuclei and disruption of thalamocortical processing.
evaluation: Claims C10-C11, C32, C35-C36, C53, and C74-C83 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature on adult anesthesia EEG patterns and computational models (Purdon et al., 2013; Vijayan et al., 2013; Akeju et al., 2014c; Cimenser et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2012; Ching et al., 2010; Brown et al., 2011; Feshchenko et al., 2004; Murphy et al., 2011; Ní Mhuircheartaigh et al., 2013; Akeju et al., 2014b). These claims provide important context for interpreting the infant findings.

result: The manuscript reviews prior pediatric anesthesia EEG studies by Davidson et al. (2008), Lo et al. (2009), Hayashi et al. (2012), and Sury et al. (2014), describing their methodologies and key findings regarding age-dependent EEG changes during anesthesia and emergence.
evaluation: Claims C64-C73 accurately summarize findings from cited prior studies (Davidson et al., 2008; Lo et al., 2009; Hayashi et al., 2012; Sury et al., 2014). These claims provide appropriate context for how the current study builds upon and refines previous pediatric anesthesia EEG research.

result: The study demonstrates that infants 0-6 months of age have markedly different EEG patterns from each other and from adults under general anesthesia, and these differences help explain why EEG-based indices provide inaccurate measures of anesthetic states in children, especially during the first three months of life.
evaluation: Claims C93 and C95 are supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing age-dependent differences in EEG patterns. The inference that these differences explain the inaccuracy of adult-derived EEG indices in infants is logical and well-supported, though the study does not directly test EEG-based indices.

result: The study collected continuous multichannel EEG recordings from 36 infants aged 0-6 months during awake state, MOSSA, and emergence from sevoflurane anesthesia. After exclusions, 30 infants were included in MOSSA analysis (11 aged 0-3 months, 19 aged 4-6 months) and 24 in emergence analysis (8 aged 0-3 months, 16 aged 4-6 months). Median end-tidal sevoflurane concentrations during MOSSA were 2.0% (95% CI: 0.8-2.6%) for 0-3 months and 2.6% (95% CI: 2.4-3.1%) for 4-6 months.
evaluation: Claims C96-C100 describe the study design, enrollment, and clinical parameters, which are supported by Figure 1, Figure 2, and Table 1. The sample sizes are modest but reasonable for an observational study in this population. The exclusion criteria and reasons for exclusions are clearly documented.
